title: Do Japan’s new single-minded convenience store bento show depressing poverty or satisfying focus?
description: The line between simplicity and inadequacy can be a fine one. Which side do Lawson’s new Ittentoppasugi fall on? 9 times out of 10, there’s an excited spring in our step as we walk through the door of our local Japanese convenience store on the release day for a new bento boxed lunch. As we […]
content:
The line between simplicity and inadequacy can be a fine one. Which side do Lawson’s new Ittentoppasugi fall on?

9 times out of 10, there’s an excited spring in our step as we walk through the door of our local Japanese convenience store on the release day for a new bento boxed lunch. As we crossed over the threshold into Lawson on September 22, though, our emotional state was more complicated.

Lawson is calling its newest bento series Ittentoppasugi, which basically translates to “super single-minded.” That’s a bit of a warning sign already, since a big part of the appeal of bento is that you usually get a number of different side dishes to go along with the rice that they always contain. Any pretense of variety is swept away for the Ittentoppasugi bento, which consist of rice, one topping ingredient, and absolutely nothing else.

In other words, in any individual Ittentoppasugi bento you’re only getting as much variety as you would in a rice ball with a single type of filling. Actually, even rice balls usually have a longer list of ingredients, since a lot of them come wrapped in seaweed. Because of that, a lot of the online reactions when Lawson first announced the Ittentoppasugi series wasn’t so much joy at its focus, but sadness that this is another sign of how rising prices in Japan seem to be affecting every aspect of daily life, eroding even such simple pleasures as affordable convenience store food.

With prices for conventional boxed lunches continuing to climb, the 297-yen (US$1.90) starting price for Lawson’s single-minded bento are, however, an intriguing offer for those who’ve given up on buying more expensive alternatives. So we were willing to give the new boxed lunches a try, and procured an Ittentoppasugi salmon bento and an Ittentoppasugi sausage bento for taste-testing purposes.

As you can see, there’s nothing inside the salmon bento but rice, salmon flakes, and an almost palpable sense of poverty. You do at least get quite a lot of rice, though. The total weight of the single-minded salmon bento is approximately 260 grams (9.2 ounces). We didn’t weigh the packaging or minuscule amount of salmon, but even collectively they can’t weight all that much, meaning there’s a lot more than the 160 grams of rice that’s considered the standard serving size in Japan.

And while there’s not a lot of salmon, our expectations were raised by it being bodakko. Bodakko is a kind of heavily salted salmon that’s popular in Akita Prefecture, a part of Japan that’s famous for its high-quality rice. Because it’s so salty, even a small amount of bodakko is said to make a large quantity of rice taste extra-delicious, and bento with a high rice-to-salmon ratio are kind of a regional specialty of Akita.

Taking a taste, we learned that the Ittentoppasugi bodakko bento’s salmon is considerably saltier than the flaked salmon found in most bento or rice balls, but not shockingly so. As a matter of fact, we don’t think it would overpower our taste buds even without any rice to take alternating bites of.

It’s perfectly tasty salmon, though we still could have done with a greater quantity of fish. Eating at a natural pace, we had about one-fourth of the bento’s rice left when we’d finished off the last flake of salmon, which we then had to consume by itself.

Next it was time to try the Ittentoppasugi sausage bento.

This is a premium-priced Ittentoppasugi bento, but even that means that it’s still just 397 yen. It’s also heftier than its cheaper bodakko brethren, weighing in at just over 300 grams.

The sausage Ittentoppasugi also has a stronger foundation to stand on as to Lawson’s claim that single-mindedness is its reason for existence. Sure, you still get only one non-rice element, sliced sausage, but you get a lot of it, and there’s a sort of decadence to be found in such a large quality of inexpensive meat, making this feel like a cheap indulgence more than no-other-option poverty chow.

They even spruce up the sausage a bit, dressing it with a light teriyaki-style sauce that imparts some additional savory sweetness.

There’s no way to convince your brain that either of these bento are luxury dining, but they both accomplish what they set out to do. They’re two of the most affordable and easily accessible bento boxed lunches in all of Japan, and though the ingredient list is short, everything inside those boxes tastes good, and after having tried these two Ittentoppasugi, we might have to consider trying Lawson’s upcoming single-minded corn bento too.

title: Osaka may name a district after mascot Myaku-Myaku
description: I wonder who will become Myaku-Myaku Mayor. For quite a while now, the ruling political party in Osaka Prefecture, the Japan Innovation Party (Ishin no Kai), has been wanting to change Osaka into a metropolis like Tokyo. This would mainly involve breaking Osaka City into four “special wards,” which are kinds of pseudo-cities with more […]
content:
I wonder who will become Myaku-Myaku Mayor.

For quite a while now, the ruling political party in Osaka Prefecture, the Japan Innovation Party (Ishin no Kai), has been wanting to change Osaka into a metropolis like Tokyo. This would mainly involve breaking Osaka City into four “special wards,” which are kinds of pseudo-cities with more localized governments. 

The benefit would be a reduction in government redundancy, since Osaka Prefecture and Osaka City often oversee similar services and infrastructure in the same areas such as schools, hospitals, and libraries. The downside is it would be a huge pain in the neck to redraw the map and reallocate all of the services, which is probably why the idea was shot down in two referendums over the past decade.

▼ One of the proposed ways to divide Osaka City into four special wards

The Japan Innovation Party remains undeterred, however, and is working hard to keep the dream of an Osaka Metropolis alive. It recently formed a coalition with the nation’s ruling party, the Liberal Democratic Party, with a clear goal of making Osaka Japan’s “Vice Capital,” and what better way to do that than to become more like Tokyo.

Meanwhile, in an effort to bolster more public support for the metropolis idea, the Japan Innovation Party held an online survey where citizens of Osaka would vote for what they would like the new special wards to be named. Among the more lackluster choices named after geographic locations or directions, some citizen suggested “Myakumya Ward” as a possible name for the area along the north side of the current Osaka City.

The reason for this choice is that the Japanese word for “Ward” is “Ku,” so Myakumya Ward in Japanese would be “Myakumya-ku,” nearly identical to the popular mascot of the Osaka Expo, Myaku-Myaku.

▼ Yes, all over the country there have been outbreaks of Myaku-Myaku fever.

Government officials involved in the survey weren’t sure what to do with the proposed name. On one hand, it seems to make a mockery of the whole idea. On the other hand, people love a good mockery, and since the whole purpose of this survey is to generate interest in the project, Myakumya Ward is very likely the best way to accomplish that.

The full shortlist of names is the following:

  1. Osaka Yodogawa Ward, Osaka Kita Ward, Osaka Chuo Ward, Osaka Tennoji Ward
  2. Shin-Osaka Ward, Umeda Ward, Namba Ward, Tennoji Ward
  3. Yumeshima Ward, Shirokita Ward, Semba Ward, Uemachi Ward
  4. Myakumya Ward, Kita Ward, Minami Ward, Harukas Ward

The second set seems like the most sensible. Most people I talk to refer to those general areas by those major train station names anyway. “Shin-Osaka” not so much, though, and looking at the options, I kind of think “Myakumya” is the best choice for that area, which contains the site of the former Expo. I would have said “Yodogawa,” but they put that meaningless “Osaka” in front of it for some reason, so “Myakumya” it is!

Reaction to the name online was mixed but significantly leaning towards the opinion that naming a municipal district after a gooey creature is a bad idea.

“It would be embarrassing to have to write ‘Myakumyaku’ on official documents.”
“Eh, I don’t live there, so I say go for it!”
“I think if they really own it wholeheartedly, it could become a good thing.”
“I think Governor Yoshimura said flat out on a livestream that it’ll never happen.”
“I like Myakumya-ku, it sounds like a land of magical monsters.”
“We can’t do that. We’d be the laughing stock of future generations.”
“They should call it Neo-Kobe.”
“The people who have to live there should have the biggest say in that.”
“Say goodbye to property values there.”
“I can’t wait to hand out business cards that say I’m from Myakumya-ku.”
“I’m expecting Fah Ward to come up soon too.”
“I live here, and I really hate this idea.”

Ultimately, we probably should respect the wishes of people who live in Myaku-Myaku Land, because they deserve to live with dignity too. Quite frankly though, Shin-Osaka (literally “New Osaka”) sounds like some kind of sci-fi Evangelion setting, and it would just be plain wrong since it’ll literally have become old Osaka at that point. Yumeshima is also the site of an upcoming integrated resort and casino, so do people really want their special ward to be named after that?

I think the people there just need to marinate on the idea a bit, and they’ll come to realize that Myakumya Ward really is the only sensible choice here.

Source: Livedoor News, Hachima Kiko

title: Osaka’s amazing budget-luxury hotel has free takoyaki, craft beer, and comedy shows
description: To truly experience the city, OMO7 Osaka is a dream stay for any traveler. When you go traveling in Japan, there are a variety of options from which to choose from, be it hot spring inns or oversized Poké Balls. For our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon, just having a bed and a roof over her […]
content:
To truly experience the city, OMO7 Osaka is a dream stay for any traveler.

When you go traveling in Japan, there are a variety of options from which to choose from, be it hot spring inns or oversized Poké Balls. For our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon, just having a bed and a roof over her head is enough to keep her happy, but several of her friends continued to sing the praises of the OMO brand of hotels run by Hoshino Resorts (operator of unique Japanese hotels like Nara Prison and Tomamu Ice Village), with one friend in particular passionately recommending OMO7 Osaka, and since Natsuno had some plans to visit Osaka, she took this opportunity to try it out.

OMO is based on the concept of an “exciting city center hotel” that is more than simply a place to spend time, but is packed with information and activities to enjoy the city. In fact, Natsuno’s friend has even been on a trip where its entire purpose was to stay at the hotel. The brand has a current total of 18 properties nationwide that are sub-divided into five different categories: OMO1, OMO3, OMO5, OMO7, and Airport, with each type offering different services. The former OMO1 hotels were capsule hotels for minimalistic travelers and provided local guide activities, a neighborhood map, and a comfortable common space for relaxation, but as of September 2026, there are no OMO1 hotels in operation.

The OMO3 basic hotels build on OMO1, although transitioning into individual guest rooms rather than capsules, by also including a grab-and-go breakfast, being good for casual and solo travel, and OMO5 boutique hotels feature a cafe with breakfast options, great for couples:

  • OMO3 Asakusa
  • OMO3 Tokyo Akasaka
  • OMO3 Kyoto Toji
  • OMO5 Otaru
  • OMO5 Hakodate
  • OMO5 Tokyo Otsuka
  • OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda
  • OMO5 Yokohama Bashamichi
  • OMO5 Kanazawa Katamachi
  • OMO5 Kyoto Gion
  • OMO5 Kyoto Sanjo
  • OMO5 Kumamoto
  • OMO5 Okinawa Naha

▼ The sign in front of OMO5 Gotanda in Tokyo

OMO7 is the brand’s full-service hotels, offering extensive in-house facilities, such as breakfast buffets, and a cafe, restaurant, or banquet hall:

  • OMO7 Asahikawa
  • OMO7 Yokohama
  • OMO7 Osaka
  • OMO7 Kochi

Finally, there’s the sole OMO Airport, located right next to Kansai International Airport, with an express buffet, and spa and fitness options.

As Natsuno was looking at the options available to her, she was initially planning on a room-only plan without meals, but there were also family plans with half-price for elementary school students and below, and early bird prices, so it came to about 25,000 yen (US$158.41) for a family of two adults and two children for a single night.

According to Natsuno’s friend, it’s a complete waste if you don’t take advantage of the various activities and enjoy it to the fullest from check-in to check-out, so with that in mind, Natsuno reserved the free guided tour of the nearby Shinsekai area in advance.

The nearest station is Shin-Imamiya Station on the JR and Nankai Railway lines, or the Dobutsuen-mae Station on the Osaka Metro, but this time Natsuno went by JR, and the hotel turned out to be so close that you could see it right from the station platform.

Spreading out in front of the hotel is Miyagurin, a massive green space of about 7,600 square meters (about 1.88 acres) with deck terraces and walking paths surrounding the lawn area, which gives it a sense of openness that makes it hard to believe it’s right next to the station in one of Japan’s biggest cities.

In the common space OMO Base inside the building, there is a gigantic board displaying a map of the surrounding neighborhood.

It introduces spots and shops not often found in guidebooks, gathered by staff who have actually walked around the city, so it serves as a base for exploring the city in a way that you might not have found otherwise.

There are also unique photo items, such as leopard print outfits of the infamous Osaka Obachan aunties, and food samples of kushikatsu (deep-fried skewers).

Also, the quintessential Osaka beverage mixed juice was prepared as a welcome drink. Originating in Shinsekai, the exact same neighborhood as the hotel, classic Osaka mixed juice incorporates milk, crushed ice, and fruits, giving it a thick and rich milkshake-like texture.

Even though the Osakan vibe was embedded throughout, the overall atmosphere didn’t feel cluttered, but rather refined, making for a truly exquisite balance.

Before check-in, it’s possible to leave your luggage in one of the free self-service lockers, decorated by various types of kushikatsu.

There are many wonderful rooms within the hotel, but…

… the room that Natsuno stayed in was the Dandan Room, and she stepped through the door with excitement and nervous anticipation.

Natsuno was greeted with a space resembling a secret base, with beds arranged in two levels, both upper and lower, like a fancy bunk bed.

While certainly looking like a room that kids would instantly fall in love with, Natsuno couldn’t help but admit that she also loved the room a lot.

Despite how large the furniture was, it didn’t feel cramped, and by the window was a spacious sofa that could be unfolded and used as a bed. Natsuno remarked on how stylish it was, and how it was the kind of space that would make you think, “I want to live in a house like this.”

From a parent’s perspective, the fact that the upper bunk is securely enclosed gave Natsuno peace of mind for when her children were sleeping there, and having a large space for luggage was also fantastic.

With a family, the entryway easily gets cluttered with the assortment of shoes being left there, but in this room, the entryway was spacious enough that this wouldn’t become a problem, and having separate bathroom and toilet facilities was a welcome addition.

Plus, the room came stocked with Osaka-style coffee and candies.

Stylish yet easy to use, and on top of that, it brings a sense of excitement. Natsuno soon felt completely comfortable relaxing in her room.

Usually costing an additional 1,000 yen, Natsuno got a glimpse of the public bath area that almost felt like it was an art museum. Even better was that the hotel does not discriminate based on tattoos, allowing tattooed customers use of the bathing facilities, unless the hotel feels the tattoos might cause discomfort to other guests.

However, the true potential of OMO7 Osaka is not limited to just this.

Natsuno had signed up for the free tour exploring Shinsekai, including the Tsutenkaku Tower and Janjan Yokocho, an alley crowded with little eateries and wonders of the past.

The tour was led by a Go-Kinjo (“Neighborhood”) Guide OMO Ranger who knows the area inside out.

The Ranger pointed out details you would miss if you walked by yourselves, recommended shops, and even places that might look a bit intimidating to enter.

Along the way, there was even an experience where you wear clothing typical of an Osaka Obachan to take photos and receive ame-chan (“candies”) at the end. The tour was a wonderfully fun experience and Natsuno highly recommends everyone try it out if they have the time.

There are other activities you can join without reservations, as well as ones that require bookings or have a fee. Natsuno’s friend apparently joined a tour to enjoy kushikatsu and a morning tour themed around dashi (soup stock), which they claimed was “awesome.” Rather than just staying overnight, the hotel creates an opportunity to step out into the town.

At night, Natsuno headed to the guests-only event Osaka Pikapika Night.

When night falls, lantern lights illuminate Miyagurin and Pikapika Yokocho appears, where in addition to delicacies like takoyaki and craft beer, you can also enjoy nostalgic games like target shooting and smart ball, a simpler pinball variant that is also similar to pachinko.

Even for room-only stays, guests elementary school age and above are handed three tickets each, structured so you can choose two items you like from options such as takoyaki, seasonal sweets, or craft beer, and choose one of the games.

To Natsuno, it did not have the atmosphere of a mere cheap service added on as a tacky marketing ploy. The space itself was special: the lawn, the hotel’s giant exterior wall, and the lantern lights all seemed to become one, making it enjoyable just being there.

On top of that, what Natsuno personally loved the most was the main event: Kotekote Show Time.

Comedians from the entertainment company Yoshimoto Kogyo (home to groups like Downtown, Kamaitachi, Chidori, and even All Hanshin Kyojin) and OMO Rangers appear, putting on comedy live shows and a giant bingo utilizing the exterior surface of the hotel wall, which of course hotel guests can enjoy for free as well.

Children and adults alike get excited together, and you can even participate in a simple Osaka-style bon dance. At the end, Natsuno even got a commemorative photo taken with the comedian group Ambitious. It was all too much fun.

Check-out the following day was at 11:00 a.m., so Natsuno spent the morning relaxing, reading books in the facility’s Library Lounge and trying out different stylish chairs to compare them.

Even though she was just relaxing inside the hotel, Natsuno felt like she was spending time a little more mindfully than usual, and experiencing the essence of Osaka at the same time.

In the end, Natsuno stayed right up until the check-out deadline, leaving the hotel while thinking, “I don’t want to go home at all.”

After checking out, soap bubbles and a ring toss game appeared, to which Natsuno really couldn’t say no to having a go at.

On her way out, Natsuno made sure to take a copy of the free booklet that introduces OMO locations nationwide.

Now, Natsuno feels like she can completely understand why her friend stays at one OMO after another. It seems that her friend is now targeting OMO5 Kanazawa Katamachi, but Natsuno has yet to decide where she will end up going, now having become a total fan of OMO.

Hotel information
OMO7 Osaka by Hoshino Resort / OMO7大阪 by 星野リゾート

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Pokémon collaboration with Pikachu Latte and exclusive goods
description: Pokémon + Starbucks takes us on an epic coffee adventure, and now we want to catch ’em all. Starbucks Japan is famous for its exclusive limited-edition goods, and this claim to fame is now set to catapult even further, thanks to a massive new team-up with Pokémon. This new collaboration is one of the biggest […]
content:
Pokémon + Starbucks takes us on an epic coffee adventure, and now we want to catch ’em all.

Starbucks Japan is famous for its exclusive limited-edition goods, and this claim to fame is now set to catapult even further, thanks to a massive new team-up with Pokémon. This new collaboration is one of the biggest we’ve ever seen, with 41 goods adorned in original artwork, and a special Pikachu Honey Cream Latte inviting customers to “Embark on a coffee adventure with Pokémon”.

There’s a lot to get through in this new adventure, so let’s start by taking a look at the star beverage, created from a winning recipe selected from a nationwide Starbucks barista competition that received more than 700 entries. The winning recipe was submitted by Junko Nitta of Starbucks Coffee Koriyama Asaka.

▼ Nitta’s win made her the champion of the Pokémon + Starbucks Barista Battle.

The Pikachu Honey Cream Latte combines espresso with caramel and honey, creating bright yellow hues to mimic Pikachu’s colouring, while the honey-flavoured whipped cream on top is scattered with heart-shaped pieces inspired by the character’s red cheeks. According to Starbucks, the coffee flavours have been gently reined in so the drink can even be enjoyed by people who don’t usually drink coffee.


The drink is available in a Tall size only, priced at 678 yen (US$4.29) to go or 690 yen for dine-in, and every customer who purchases it will receive an original collaboration sticker, while stocks last.

Moving on to the accompanying Pokémon + Starbucks goods, they’re all adorned in artwork unique to the collaboration, created by illustrator Hikaru Ichijo. By incorporating Ichijo’s signature style of not depicting faces, the artwork covers 12 scenes where Pokémon and baristas build connections through coffee, showing us how new encounters and communities are born when diverse personalities are accepted.

The artwork welcomes us into a whole world of new discoveries, designed to take us through new adventures. Let’s take a look at how the story unfolds through this unique collection of goods, starting with the items that are available in-store from 30 September.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Reusable Cup Coffee Connection 473 millilitres (1,300 yen [US$8.18])

This reusable cup features original Pokémon + Starbucks collaboration artwork showing a barista, with Poké Ball in hand, surrounded by Pikachu, Bulbasaur, Charmander, Squirtle and Eevee, all building connections around a cup of coffee.

▼ The green circle, which harks back to Starbucks’ mermaid logo, is said to “symbolise the moment of co-creation“.

▼ The back of the cup features a collaboration-themed customisation box…

▼…while the cup itself is easy to use and comes with a removable lid for stress-free cleaning.

There are three Starbucks Cards featuring original artwork created for the collaboration, all available with a minimum 2,000 yen deposit.

▼ Coffee Connection

▼ Pikachu

▼ Eevee

Now let’s take a look at the goods that are available at Starbucks Japan’s official online store, starting with the Pokémon + Starbucks Stainless Steel To Go Bottle 473 millilitres (6,600 yen) , which comes in six designs.

▼ Pikachu


▼ All these cup-shaped stainless steel bottles have lockable lids that can be opened by sliding the button and pressing it in.

▼ They’re also resistant to leaks and easy to clean.

▼ Bulbasaur

▼ Charmander


▼ Squirtle

▼ Eevee

▼ Coffee Connection

Next up, we have the Pokémon + Starbucks Stainless Steel Bottle (473 millilitres [6,600 yen]) , which comes in five laser-engraved character designs.

▼Pikachu

▼ Bulbasaur

▼ Charmander


▼ Squirtle


▼ Eevee


Now we have a couple of items that go by the name “Pokémon + Starbucks 2-Way SS Cup/Holder” (355 millilitres [4,000 yen]). As the name suggests, these products can be used in two ways, by either pouring a drink directly into it or popping a takeaway cup inside it to help retain the temperature.

▼ Coffee Connection

▼ Coffee Adventure

The Pokémon + Starbucks Cold Cup Tumbler (710 millilitres [4,000 yen]) comes in two designs.

▼ Coffee Connection

▼ Coffee Adventure

The Pokémon + Starbucks 2-Way Stacking Mug (355 millilitres [3,800 yen])  comes in two designs that can easily be stacked together for storage.

▼ Coffee Connection

▼ Coffee Adventure

Those who find the mug too large can opt for the smaller Pokémon + Starbucks 2 -Way Stacking Demi Mug (89 millilitres [2,200 yen]) , which comes in the same two designs, and is ideal for a shot of espresso.

▼ Coffee Connection

▼ Coffee Adventure

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Straw Tumbler with Strap Coffee Adventure (458 millilitres [4,800 yen])

This tumbler features a lid design that looks like a Poké Ball! The drinking straw is made of silicone, and the shoulder strap has a safety feature that detaches when pulled with force.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Ceramic Canister Coffee Connection (3,800 yen)

The ceramic canister is large enough to hold about 100 grams of Starbucks coffee beans, and it can also be used to store small items.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Heatproof Glass Mug with SS Strainer Coffee Adventure (296 millilitres [4,400 yen])

The mug comes with a stainless steel strainer, eliminating the need for paper filters and allowing coffee to be brewed easily using the mug.

▼ The mug has a beautiful, rounded shape that makes it a pleasure to hold.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Glass Drip Coffee Maker Coffee Adventure (4,900 yen)

▼ During brewing, the lid can be used as a place to set the dripper.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks SS Kettle Coffee Connection (550 millilitres [5,800 yen])

The stainless steel kettle is designed to help pour a consistent amount of water with ease.

The adventure reaches a climax in what for us is the showstopper.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Milk Frother & Cup Coffee Adventure (4,400 yen)

This three-piece set includes a milk frother and heatproof glass mug for making lattes and cappuccinos at home, with a cap to prevent splashes.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Utility Apron Coffee Connection (4,800 yen)

The utility apron features Coffee Connection artwork on one front pocket and a collaboration logo and customisation box on the other.

▼ The rivets feature embossed Poké Ball motifs.

The apron comes in warm grey and can be used for all sorts of everyday activities, including DIY and kitchen work.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Kids Apron Pikachu (4,000 yen)

Recommended for heights of 100–120 centimetres (39.37 to 47.24 inches), the kids’ apron features artwork of a barista and Pikachu displaying the skills they’ve developed together.

▼ The side hem features the collaboration logo and customisation box.

▼ The apron is a vivid yellow inspired by Pikachu, and the neck strap can be removed using a buckle on the side.

Moving out of the kitchen, we have a range of stickers, postcards and art posters that focus on the original collaboration art.

The Pokémon + Starbucks Art Sticker Set (1,800 yen) contains 13 stickers featuring all 12 original artworks, including three cup-inspired designs, which are a good size for decorating small items and smartphones.

The Pokémon + Starbucks Art Postcard Set (2,000 yen) gives you 12 designs that can be used as postcards or displayed as miniature artworks.

There are also two Pokémon + Starbucks Art Posters (2,500 yen each) that blow the art up to 28 x 35-centimetre (11 x 14-inch) proportions, giving you a unique way to display your love of coffee and Pokémon in your home.

▼ Coffee Connection

▼ Coffee Adventure

You don’t have to be at home to enjoy the new collection, as there’s a range of tote bags and pouches that are perfect for daily adventures out in the wild.

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Tote Bag Coffee Connection (5,000 yen)

▼ Pokémon + Starbucks Tote Bag Coffee Adventure (5,000 yen)

The Pokémon + Starbucks Cup-Shaped PVC Pouch (2,200 yen)  comes in five character designs, with the front side depicting each Pokémon displaying the skills they’ve developed with their partner barista, while the rear features a collaboration ID box and logo.

▼ Pikachu

 ▼ The pouch is large enough to hold a smartphone and can be attached to a bag using the carabiner.

▼ Bulbasaur

▼ Charmander

▼ Squirtle

▼ Eevee

To help dress up the totes and pouches, there are two Pokémon + Starbucks Acrylic Charms (1,500 yen each) that can be easily attached to them.

title: Fukushima’s popular dialect T-shirt vending machine gets its first sibling in Iwaki
description: Pick up a wearable Japanese lesson featuring dinosaurs, hot springs, and deep sea fish. Following the 2011 disaster, Fukushima Prefecture has steadily worked to rebuild its tourism appeal, offering a region filled with natural beauty and history to travelers who seek to venture beyond Japan’s Golden Route of Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, and sometimes Hiroshima. In […]
content:
Pick up a wearable Japanese lesson featuring dinosaurs, hot springs, and deep sea fish.

Following the 2011 disaster, Fukushima Prefecture has steadily worked to rebuild its tourism appeal, offering a region filled with natural beauty and history to travelers who seek to venture beyond Japan’s Golden Route of Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, and sometimes Hiroshima. In the coastal city of Iwaki, known for its Aquamarine Fukushima aquarium and the tropical Spa Resort Hawaiians, a new attraction at JR Iwaki Station’s S-Pal shopping center offers a fun way to connect with the area, and return with a unique souvenir.

Building on the popularity of the original Fukushima dialect t-shirt vending machine at JR Fukushima Station, this latest Iwaki installment brings the wearable local culture directly to coastal visitors.

▼ The Fukushima Station designs: five for each of the three regions of the prefecture

When people think of Japanese dialects, Kansai-ben from the Kansai region centered around Osaka usually comes to mind. However, Japan features a rich array of regional dialects (hogen, 方言), each reflecting distinct local history and geography. Fukushima itself is divided into three cultural and linguistic zones: Hamadori (the coast, where Iwaki is located), Nakadori (the central valley, home to Fukushima and Koriyama cities), and Aizu (the western mountains, famed for Tsuruga Castle, Kitakata-style ramen, and Higashiyama Hot Spring). Each region boasts its own endearing vocabulary and idioms that sound remarkably different from standard Tokyo Japanese.

These local expressions have become the focus of the Fukushima Dialect T-shirts. Priced at 2,000 yen (US$12.69), each shirt pairs regional phrases with charming illustrations, and the Iwaki vending machine offers a selection of 12 designs that are inspired by local icons and differ from the 15 found in Fukushima’s vending machine.

These coastal Hamadori designs highlight phrases like appatoppa (あっぱとっぱ, “confused” or “flustered”), which features the locally discovered Futabasaurus, and koderanni (こでらんに, “the best” or “can’t get enough of [it]”), depicting Shiramizu Amidado, one of the oldest and most important temples in the Tohoku region.

There are also four designs that showcase beloved Iwaki icons: the mehikari (bigeyed greeneye fish), anko (anglerfish that is used in the traditional hot pot dish anko nabe), hula dance, and Iwaki Yumoto hot spring.

▼ Hula dance helped save the town in the mid-1960s after the local mines closed.

Adding to the excitement, the vending machine operates like a mystery capsule, so after selecting your size of medium, large, or extra large, a random design from the collection is dispensed.

▼ Mehikari are delicious both eaten raw and deep-fried

For both domestic and international visitors, these local dialect mystery T-shirts will serve as warm reminders of your time spent in this region, and be a great conversation starter with Japanese locals wherever you travel. So, whether you are playing to delve into samurai heritage at Tsuraga Castle, walk through the thatched roof village of Ouchijuku, explore the beautiful highlands of Bandai, or enjoy Iwaki’s Pacific coast, consider making a little detour and grabbing one of these T-shirts from the station vending machine, so you can carry it home and wear a slice of Fukushima’s charm.

title: Japanese airport offering 19,250-yen sandwiches as last Japan meal for international travelers
description: If you want one last taste of Japanese luxury, Kansai International Airport has a restaurant that says it can give it to you in just five minutes. With delicious food being one of the major things that draws travelers to Japan, many people are going to want to splurge on something luxurious for their last […]
content:
If you want one last taste of Japanese luxury, Kansai International Airport has a restaurant that says it can give it to you in just five minutes.

With delicious food being one of the major things that draws travelers to Japan, many people are going to want to splurge on something luxurious for their last meal in the country. On the other hand, with Japan also having tons of non-food-related stuff to see and do, your itinerary might be so full that you don’t have time to slot in anything other than something speedy from the airport before your flight home.

However, if you’re flying out of Japan from Kansai International Airport in Osaka, you can get something quick and decadent…and also very expensive, since Kobist will sell you a fast food sandwich that costs 19,250 yen (US$120).

▼ Kobist

That might sound like an extreme case of airport price-gouging, but this isn’t some ordinary convenience store sandwich (although even those are pretty tasty in Japan). Kobist’s name comes from Kobe, the city with the most exalted beef pedigree in all of Japan, and arguably the world, and the 19,250-yen menu item is their large-size Kobe beef steak sandwich.

Kobist, which opened this past summer, bills itself as a “luxury fast food” restaurant, with the goal of letting travelers enjoy the flavor of authentic Kobe beef even if they only have five minutes to spare. Located inside Terminal 1, in the area past the security check-in for international departures, Kobist is a new venture from Bifteck Kawamura (also known as Bifuteki no Kawamura), a Kobe steak specialist that’s been around since 1972. The chain’s flagship restaurant is in downtown Kobe, but they also have branches in Tokyo’s swanky Ginza and Roppongi districts.

▼ Bifteck Kawamura’s flagship restaurant

So while Kobist is charging 19,250 yen for a sandwich, another way of looking at it is that they’re charging 19,250 yen for a large Kobe steak, which wouldn’t be a record-breaking price, and just serving it with bread wrapped around the meat rather than a dinner roll on the side.

And while Kobist isn’t a budget-priced eatery by any means, it does also have options quite a bit more affordable than its top-of-the-line large Kobe beef steak sandwich. The regular-size version, for example, is about half that price (9,900 yen), and the restaurant also has hamburgers starting at 3,300 yen and steak sandwiches from 3,850 yen made with other types of wagyu/Japanese beef.

Sure, none of those are a highly cost-effective way to fill up before your long flight home, but for meat-loving travelers who don’t know when, or if, they’ll be back in in the country, Kobist would definitely make for a memorable last Japan meal.

Restaurant information
Kobist
Address: Osaka-fu, Izumisano-shi, Senshu Kuko Kita 1, Kansai International Airport Terminal 1 Building, 2nd floor
大阪府泉佐野市泉州空港北1関西国際空港第1ターミナルビル２F
Open 6:30 a.m.-12:55 a.m.

title: US$9,700 solid-gold Pokémon figure going on sale in Japan, life-size gold-leaf Pikachu appears too
description: Artisans create an extremely expensive, and extremely accurate, recreation of a certain Steel/Ghost-type Pokémon. If you’re lucky enough to find an interest in your youth that you can enjoy into your adult years, and also fortunate enough to secure a grown-up job that allows some extra room in your budget for fun stuff, you’ll eventually […]
content:
Artisans create an extremely expensive, and extremely accurate, recreation of a certain Steel/Ghost-type Pokémon.

If you’re lucky enough to find an interest in your youth that you can enjoy into your adult years, and also fortunate enough to secure a grown-up job that allows some extra room in your budget for fun stuff, you’ll eventually find yourself in a situation where you’re pondering splurging on your hobby. Sure, that anime/video game figure is expensive, but it looks cool, and it’ll make you happy, so why not go for it? Live a little!

However, even relatively well-to-do Pokémon fans will probably need some extra time to mull over the series’ latest figure of Gholdengo.

If we were going by looks alone, picking up this figure would be a no-brainer. According to its Pokédex entries, Gholdengo’s body is made of gold, and this figure boasts an appropriately alluring shine. This fidelity to the source material wasn’t achieved with special paint applied to plastic, though, and is instead a result of the figure being made of solid 24-karat gold.

At 6 centimeters (2.4 inches) in height and weighing 15 grams (0.53 ounces), in terms of size and weight the 24-Karat Gholdengo would be perfect for setting on the corner of your desk to mingle with whatever capsule toys or acrylic mini standees reside there. Price-wise, though? This probably deserves a special place where it’s less likely to get knocked off its perch, since the asking price is 1.54 million yen (approximately US$9,700).

That price tag is going to bump the solid-gold Gholdengo out of the reasonable-to-buy range for many fans, but it’s still in the awesome-to-look-at category, and so thankfully the one-of-a-kind piece will be on display at the Takashimaya department store in Yokohama, which is holding the Yokohama Grand Gold Exhibition later this month. Two other golden Pokémon figures will also be on display, a life-size Pikachu (50 centimeters tall) and a life-size Gholdengo (120 centimeters, according to its Pokédex entry).

Instead of being solid gold, the life-size figures are covered in gold leaf, with roughly 200 sheets used for Pikachu and 730 for Gholdengo. Neither one is being offered for sale at the event.

The exhibition will also feature many non-Pokémon pieces, with over 1,000 gold items being shown by participating artisans, such as golden orin singing bowls and figurines of the upcoming Chinese Zodiac animal, the sheep.

The Yokohama Grand Gold Exhibition takes place from September 30 to October 5 in the special event area on the 8th floor of the Yokohama Takashimaya, located right outside Yokohama Station. Admission is free, by the way, so if you’re right on the borderline of being able to afford that solid-gold Gholdengo, at least you don’t have to worry about paying for a ticket.

title: Sanrio to release own rhythm game for smartphones next January
description: Hello, tired fingers. Sometimes I wonder if there’s a corner of existence that Hello Kitty and her friends from Sanrio haven’t established a presence in. Electric guitars? Check. Gundam? Check. Haunted zombie land? Check. But one place Hello Kitty has yet to appear is a smartphone-exclusive rhythm game (Taiko no Tatsujin doesn’t count because that […]
content:
Hello, tired fingers.

Sometimes I wonder if there’s a corner of existence that Hello Kitty and her friends from Sanrio haven’t established a presence in. Electric guitars? Check. Gundam? Check. Haunted zombie land? Check.

But one place Hello Kitty has yet to appear is a smartphone-exclusive rhythm game (Taiko no Tatsujin doesn’t count because that cameo was on a console version). However, that small patch of reality will soon go without kawaii cats and puppies no longer as Sanrio Kawaii Me Live! is set to be released in January 2027.

In this game, a range of characters from Sanrio’s vast roster, including Hello Kitty, My Melody, Pompompurin, Cinnamoroll, Kuromi, and many more, perform on stage with your help. There are two styles of rhythm play: one involves tapping at the right time when two circles converge in a style somewhat similar to the dance-offs in Final Fantasy VII Remake or Yakuza 0. The other style requires keeping your finger along a horizontal bar and tapping or sliding it on the objects as they fall in a style like Guitar Hero or Beatmania.

The game is free to play, and you’ll get to start off with Sanrio’s own playlist of seven songs based on their characters. There will also be collaboration songs with Polkadot Stingray, Soala, Mi’Line Hearts, Yabai T-Shirts Yasan, Lienel, She’s, and Zutomayo. More songs will also be added over time.

But the real charm in Sanrio Kawaii Me Live! is to do as the title suggests and kawaii up your chosen character. Unlock new outfits and musical equipment for your character to wear and hold, while also designing the stage layout to your personal preference. It seems like any Sanrio fan would want to spend most of their time in this part of the game, but you’ll have to perform to unlock more costumes.

Also, for people in Yokohama, there will be a chance to experience the fun live at a release event on 14 January, 2027 at Yokohama Kannai Hall. There will be live performances by many of the artists mentioned above, and appearances by many of the Sanrio characters mentioned above.

In the meantime, pre-registration for the game is already underway on the App Store and Google Play Store. And to make sure no one dawdles, Sanrio Games is holding a special campaign to unlock in-game items based on how many people pre-register, starting with an energy-boosting Cosmo Soda item at 50,000 people, up to a Hello Kitty dressed in Mira Wear if one million people promise to check out the game.

▼ Mira Wear Hello Kitty

There’s still a way to go before the release of Sanrio Kawaii Me Live! and more details are sure to emerge before then. It seems to me that this title is ripe for Yoshikitty to make an appearance, either as an unlockable character or final boss where you’ll have to wear your fingers out trying to tap through “Kurenai.”
